subject: Post-call: Acme performance/SLO & concurrency + Redwood rate limits
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: John Wu <john.wu@acme.com>; Priya Singh <priya.singh@acme.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 25 Nov 2026 14:10:00 -0800
Subject: Post-call recap: Acme performance/SLO & concurrency

Thanks again for the time today — great conversation. Quick recap and next steps so we have alignment on the performance/SLO requirements and concurrency expectations before I loop in finance for a formal quote.

Key notes from the call:
- Latency SLO: 95th percentile <= 350ms for short completions (~50 tokens); 95th <= 700ms for streaming large outputs (500-1k tokens)
- Throughput: steady-state 600 requests/minute during business hours, burst to 2,500 requests/minute for 10-15 minute spikes
- Concurrency: application sends up to 250 parallel requests (connection pooling from multiple web servers); expect ~20k open connections behind a pooling layer
- Streaming: client requires incremental tokens (server->client) with low tail latency; ability to preserve KV-cache across session replays is important

Questions / asks for next steps:
1) Can you confirm whether the 250 parallel requests are per-region or global? (We discussed primarily US.)
2) Do you need soft limits during pilot vs committed quotas for production? If so, what level of guaranteed concurrency are you expecting in an initial committed contract?
3) Please attach your traffic sample (1-2 hours preferred) and any existing load test results.

Attachments: I’ve attached a short template to capture peak windows and traffic shape (acme-performance-requirements.xlsx).

Next steps:
- Laura (cc) will follow up with technical guidance on connection handling and recommended Redwood rate-limit config.
- I’ll draft a committed quota proposal and an initial quote for the concurrency tier we discussed.
- John/Priya to share traffic samples and any compliance constraints.

Thanks,
Marissa
Account Executive | Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com

Attachment: acme-performance-requirements.xlsx (spreadsheet stub)

From: John Wu <john.wu@acme.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@acme.com>
Date: Thu, 26 Nov 2026 09:22:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Acme performance/SLO & concurrency

Thanks, Marissa — that recap matches our notes. A few clarifications from our side: 
- Concurrency scope: The 250 parallel requests is per-application cluster (we run two active clusters in US-east and US-west; traffic is roughly 70/30 split). We expect to route requests regionally, so please treat 250 as per-cluster.
- For pilot, we want a soft quota of 500 concurrent requests (across both clusters) and production committed quota of 1,000 concurrent requests with an ability to burst to 2,000 for 5-10 minutes.
- Streaming: we need sub-200ms first-byte for streaming starts on typical prompts; tail can be higher but target 95th <= 700ms as noted.

I’ve attached our load test csv (throughput-test-results.csv) and a short network diagram. We can share more telemetry if needed.

On pricing: we’re sensitive to unit cost. If you can provide a committed concurrency tier discount or a monthly reserved capacity SKU that guarantees 1,000 concurrent connections, that would help our procurement team.

John
Head of Product Engineering | Acme Corp
john.wu@acme.com

Attachment: throughput-test-results.csv (CSV stub)

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
To: John Wu <john.wu@acme.com>
Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@acme.com>, Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>, Nikhil Sharma <nikhil@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 27 Nov 2026 10:05:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Acme performance/SLO & concurrency

Appreciate the quick turnaround and the test results, John — helpful. Two things while we work on a formal proposal: 
- Laura / Nikhil: can you confirm feasibility of the following and suggested Redwood config?
  - Per-cluster concurrency guarantee: pilot soft 500 (shared), production committed 1,000 with burst to 2,000 for short windows
  - Connection pooling recommendation: we typically recommend a pooling layer that multiplexes fewer persistent connections to the Redwood frontend; we’ll outline suggested connection counts per pool to reduce open-socket pressure on the control plane
  - Rate limits & quotas: we can do per-account and per-route quotas; need to confirm default token-based rate limits and whether we can map to your request-rate expectations

- John: I’ll put together two pricing options: (A) reserved concurrency tier (monthly commit) that guarantees throughput and a lower per-token/unit cost, and (B) a hybrid model with a smaller commit + soft burst budget. Which finance cadence do you prefer for a procurement PO (monthly or annual)?

Thanks — will loop back with a draft quote and proposed SLO language.

Marissa

From: Laura Bennett <laura@redwood.com>
To: John Wu <john.wu@acme.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>
Cc: Nikhil Sharma <nikhil@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 16:30:00 -0800
Subject: Technical follow-up: concurrency, connection pooling, and rate-limit suggestions

Hi John — quick technical follow-up based on Marissa’s notes and your test CSV. Short answers and recommended config: 

1) Concurrency model
- We can support the approach you described (per-cluster logical concurrency). Operationally we expose:
  - concurrent_requests (logical parallel requests being handled)
  - connection_count (TCP/WebSocket connections)
- For your traffic shape (heavy short requests + periodic long streams), recommended committed profile: 1,000 concurrent_requests (production) with burst headroom up to 2,000 for 10 minutes. That maps cleanly to our Dedicated-style reserved capacity tiers.

2) Connection pooling
- Best practice: have application-level pools that maintain ~50 persistent connections per app cluster to Redwood frontends, with multiplexing on HTTP/2 or WebSocket where possible. This reduces active socket pressure — you mentioned ~20k open sockets behind your load balancers; we recommend a pooling layer so Redwood sees far fewer persistent connections (we instrument per-connection metrics).

3) Streaming requirements
- We can meet sub-200ms first-byte for streaming starts for typical prompts on the recommended reserved capacity profile. For long outputs, KV-cache reuse matters — enable session affinity (sticky routing) for clients that do replays.

4) Rate limits & quotas (how we typically structure)
- Per-account soft limits: allow short bursts above committed quota for X minutes (configurable), with graceful throttling when sustained over quota.
- Per-route (API key) hard limits: protect shared pools; we can map route limits to your per-endpoint traffic patterns.
- We’ll propose: committed concurrency = 1,000, soft-burst buffer = +1,000 for 10 minutes, auto-fallback to a compatible smaller model if capacity constrained.

5) Next steps (ops + procurement)
- Marissa: I’ll draft a short SLO clause we can include in the quote that specifies p95 latency targets, committed concurrency, and burst policy.
- John/Priya: if you can confirm preferred billing cadence and any required SLA language, we’ll finalize the pricing options.

Cheers,
Laura
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
laura@redwood.com

From: John Wu <john.wu@acme.com>

Cc: Priya Singh <priya.singh@acme.com>
Date: Mon, 30 Nov 2026 09:43:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Post-call recap: Acme performance/SLO & concurrency

All looks good — thanks for the thorough notes, team. A few final items before procurement: 
- Procurement prefers an annual reserved capacity SKU that guarantees 1,000 concurrent_requests with burst to 2,000. Can you provide a price for the annual commit (tiered bands OK)?
- We also need an explicit fallback policy in the SLO text: if Redwood triggers quota throttling more than 3x/month for >5 minutes, we need a credits remediation clause or faster escalation path.
- Please include estimated RPS and token-volume projections for each pricing option so we can map to our cost model.

If you can send a short formal quote (PDF) and the SLO language by EOD Wednesday, we’ll start internal review and plan to route to procurement the following week.

John
